turns.content: A survey records whether a respondent watched football (A), basketball (B), or baseball (C) during the same year. It reports P(A)=0.43, P(B)=0.40, P(C)=0.32, P(A intersect B)=0.29, P(A intersect C)=0.22, P(B intersect C)=0.20, and P(A intersect B intersect C)=0.15. Before calculating overall reach, explain what the marginal, pairwise-overlap, and triple-overlap probabilities represent.

For football and basketball, compare P(A intersect B) with P(A)P(B). What kind of association is suggested, and can this observational survey establish that football viewing causes basketball viewing?

For this step, use the phrase 'watched at least one of football, basketball, or baseball' to mean that the respondent watched exactly one of the three. Write the event in terms of A, B, and C under that terminology.
Treat A, B, and C as pairwise-disjoint events and write the addition formula for the probability that a respondent watched at least one of the three sports.

Treat the listed marginals and intersections as conditional survey probabilities, and substitute them into the current union formula: P(A)=0.43, P(B)=0.40, P(C)=0.32, P(A intersect B)=0.29, P(A intersect C)=0.22, P(B intersect C)=0.20, and P(A intersect B intersect C)=0.15.
Substitute the reported values into that expression and evaluate 0.43+0.40+0.32-0.29-0.22-0.20+0.15.
Check the calculation by explaining why the three pairwise intersections are subtracted and the triple intersection is added. Then interpret the resulting union probability for this surveyed group.
State the final probability that a respondent watched at least one sport, and briefly summarize what the observed overlaps do and do not establish about relationships among the viewing habits.
